content: Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, was established in 2000 as a global health partnership with the primary objective of ensuring equitable access to new and underutilized vaccines for children in the world's poorest countries. Its mission includes accelerating vaccine access, strengthening national health and immunization systems, and introducing innovative immunization technologies. Gavi collaborates with countries to scale up domestically funded immunization efforts. As countries achieve economic growth, Gavi requires them to gradually assume more financial responsibility until they can fully transition out of Gavi's support. Regional Immunization Technical Advisory Groups (RITAGs) have been established in each of the six WHO regions—Africa, the Americas, Eastern Mediterranean, Europe, South-East Asia, and Western Pacific. These groups provide recommendations to WHO Regional Directors and countries on immunization priorities and strategies, tailored to regional epidemiological and social contexts. National Immunization Technical Advisory Groups (NITAGs) are multidisciplinary groups of national experts that offer independent, evidence-based advice to policymakers and program managers on immunization and vaccine-related policy issues. The adaptation of WHO's Strategic Advisory Group of Experts (SAGE) guidance occurs at both regional and national levels, with WHO encouraging the contextualization of global guidance by RITAGs and NITAGs, considering local disease epidemiology, resource availability, and regional or national priorities. The GRADE-ADOLOPMENT approach combines adoption, adaptation, and, when necessary, de novo development of recommendations. This method uses the GRADE evidence-to-decision frameworks and criteria to determine the direction and strength of recommendations, enabling users to create context-appropriate guidance. By transparently presenting research evidence and associated judgments, regional and national advisory groups can facilitate the adoption of recommendations by other stakeholders. Vaccine monitoring and evaluation systems are essential for collecting and analyzing data on vaccination coverage and other indicators, such as the implementation of WHO-recommended policies. WHO uses these data to assess the impact of vaccination policies. In the context of the Immunization Agenda 2030 (IA2030), the monitoring and evaluation (M&E) framework provides action-based indicators to track progress toward IA2030 goals and strategic objectives. This framework includes tailored indicators to enable data-driven improvements in immunization programs at all levels. Underlying the three impact goals of IA2030 are seven impact goal indicators to monitor progress across country, regional, and global levels. The M&E framework also offers strategic priority objectives and indicator options for regions and countries to develop their own M&E frameworks. Since 1998, WHO and UNICEF have jointly collected immunization data through the standardized Joint Reporting Form (JRF), which was updated in 2021 to a cloud-based electronic Joint Reporting Form (eJRF). The eJRF collects annual immunization data from countries, helping identify trends and gaps at country, regional, and global levels. The data collected through the eJRF are critical for tracking the implementation of SAGE-related strategies and policies worldwide, monitoring improvements, and identifying areas for evaluation. WHO generally issues evidence-based recommendations for vaccine use after a vaccine has received regulatory approval from a National Regulatory Authority (NRA) of maturity level 3 or higher, or when it is undergoing WHO prequalification or Emergency Use Listing (EUL). The regulatory and prequalification processes are independent but involve overlapping data requirements. Regulatory decision-making focuses on product quality, manufacturing consistency, safety, and efficacy, while immunization policy decision-making considers clinical data, population protection, programmatic feasibility, equity, ethical considerations, and health economics. The WHO Expert Committee on Biological Standardization (ECBS) provides recommendations and guidelines for the manufacturing, licensing, and control of vaccines and other biological products. These guidelines ensure the quality, safety, and efficacy of vaccines and are applied during the prequalification review process. National Regulatory Authorities (NRAs) and national control laboratories play a critical role in regulatory oversight, testing, and releasing WHO-prequalified vaccines. WHO prequalification ensures that vaccines used in immunization programs are safe, effective, and programmatically suitable. Manufacturers can apply for prequalification if their vaccine meets specific criteria, including inclusion on the vaccine prequalification priority list, compliance with programmatic suitability requirements, and regulatory approval from an NRA of maturity level 3 or higher. The WHO Emergency Use Listing (EUL) procedure is a risk-based process for assessing and listing unlicensed vaccines, therapeutics, and diagnostics to expedite their availability during public health emergencies of international concern (PHEIC) or graded global emergencies. The EUL process assists UN procurement agencies and Member States in determining the acceptability of using specific products based on available data on quality, safety, efficacy, and programmatic suitability. Products eligible for EUL must address serious or life-threatening diseases, comply with good manufacturing practices, and have regulatory oversight from an NRA of maturity level 3 or higher. Applicants must commit to completing product development and applying for WHO prequalification once the product is licensed. Providing policy guidance on vaccine use and immunization-related topics across diverse geographical and cultural contexts is a challenging but essential public health endeavor. This process must be grounded in the highest quality scientific evidence. The approaches outlined in this guidance reflect the consensus of immunization experts on applying rigorous methods to evaluate scientific evidence. Transparency is crucial throughout the policy development process, and this document aims to enhance the transparency and standardization of WHO vaccine and immunization recommendations. It will be regularly updated as improvements are identified and methodologies evolve.
